papers.title_in_file: Quantum vs. Classical Machine Learning: A Unified Empirical Comparison
papers.what_it_is: An empirical comparison of seven quantum and classical model pairs on a Bars and Stripes classification dataset and a hypercube reinforcement learning task, run on a noiseless simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical models outperform the evaluated QML models in overall accuracy, policy stability and training efficiency across both the classification and the sequential decision-making tasks.
quotes: Classical machine learning (CML) models currently outperform the evaluated QML models in terms of overall accuracy, policy stability, and training efficiency across both classification and sequential decision-making tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: One study on one synthetic classification dataset and one custom environment; Tables 1 and 2, p.9.
assertions.reader_inference: Result holds only for the small, deliberately parameter-matched, noiseless-simulator setup; it says little about hardware or larger models.

assertions.value: The authors state that all quantum circuits are evaluated on a noiseless state-vector simulator, and that the study covers seven model pairs on a Bars and Stripes dataset and a Hypercube Environment.
quotes: we evaluate seven representative model pairs across classification tasks and sequential decision-making tasks.
all quantum circuits are evaluated on a noiseless state-vector
All classification models are evaluated on the same BAS dataset
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup, Section 3.4, p.6.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QCNN reached a precision of 0.9014 against 0.8537 for its classical CNN counterpart on the BAS dataset, while QML models generally trail in recall.
quotes: the Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) achieves a notably higher precision (0.9014) compared to its classical CNN counterpart (0.8537)
While QML generally trails in recall, specific architectural designs demonstrate superior specificity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single run on one synthetic dataset, Table 1.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 shows the QCNN with accuracy 0.8187 against 0.8250 for the CNN, so the precision edge comes with lower recall and slightly lower accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QQL agent reached a 94.0% win rate with 66 parameters, against a 100% win rate with 422 parameters for the classical baseline.
quotes: The Quantum Q-Learning (QQL) agent achieves a 94.0% win rate using only 66 parameters
reduction compared to the classical baseline (422 parameters, 100% win rate).
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study; Table 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The same table shows QQL training time and return stability far worse than the classical agent, so the parameter saving is offset elsewhere.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I, II, III (results text), V Conclusion; Section IV (circuit QED platform) skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper showing that a bound state in the agent-noise energy spectrum restores the performance of a single two-level-system quantum reinforcement learning eigensolver under non-Markovian noise.

assertions.value: The authors report that the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum of the agent-noise system restores the QRL performance to that of the noiseless case.
quotes: we find that the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum of the total agent-noise system restores the QRL performance to that in the noiseless case.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytical derivation checked by numerical simulation for one model; no theorem is stated.
assertions.reader_inference: The result concerns a single two-level agent coupled to a bosonic bath, not a general QML workload.

assertions.value: The authors report that, without the bound state, the mean fidelity saturates to 0.8.
quotes: we find that the mean fidelity Ft saturates to 0.8 in the absence of the bound state
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation, Fig. 3(b).

assertions.value: The authors state that the work aims to highlight the noise-resilient mechanism rather than to present an efficient algorithm, and that the analysis is restricted to a two-level system.
assertions.anchor: Section II, p.2; Section V, p.7
quotes: our work aims to highlight the underlying noise-resilient mechanism, rather than presenting an efficient algorithm.
we restrict our analysis to a two-level system
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V, p.7, states the scope and limit.

papers.title_in_file: A Versatile Variational Quantum Kernel Framework for Non-Trivial Classification
papers.version_note: File name says Benchmarking Quantum Kernels; the title inside the file matches the record (Jiang Yuhan and Otten).
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I, II (design), IV, V, VI; Section III and appendices skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A classical-simulation benchmark of trainable variational quantum kernels against linear and RBF kernels on eight real-world datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that their quantum kernels reach competitive classification accuracy against standard classical kernels, in classical simulation, on eight real-world, high-dimensional datasets.
quotes: We conducted a comprehensive benchmark of this framework on eight challenging, real-world and high-dimensional datasets
Our results show that the proposed quantum kernels demonstrate competitive classification accuracy compared to standard classical kernels in classical simulation
demonstrate marginal but consistent performance gains over standard classical kernels across a diverse set of complex, real-world machine learning tasks
assertions.certainty_reason: One study; Table I.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors tuned quantum kernels under a constrained search and classical kernels by grid search; the gains are described as marginal.

assertions.value: The authors state that on the SEED-P12S1 dataset QAmp outperformed the best classical kernel (Linear) by about 30% relative.
quotes: On the SEED-P12S1 dataset, QAmp outperformed the best classical kernel (Linear) by about 30% relative.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, Table I.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I as extracted shows equal results for all kernels on SEED-P12S1 and the large gain (0.6843 for Linear, 0.8780 for QAmp) on PhysioNet2017-NA, so the text appears to name the wrong dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results were obtained in the idealized infinite-shot limit on a statevector simulator, and that performance on real quantum devices remains a next step.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.B, p.6; Section VI, p.9; Abstract
quotes: Furthermore, our results were obtained in the idealized infinite-shot limit.
A next step is to determine the performance on real quantum devices
Further research is needed to fully assess the practical performance of quantum methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors in Section VI, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used two qubits (a four-dimensional Hilbert space) for the truncated RBF kernel, after reducing sample size and feature dimension with PCA and a classical learning curve.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A.2, p.3; Section IV.A, p.5
quotes: Based on preliminary analysis, here we use two qubits that form a four-dimensional Hilbert space, which we found to be sufficient
we conducted an explained variance analysis using Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup.

papers.title_in_file: Option Pricing on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers: A Quantum Neural Network Approach
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections 1, 3, 6, 7, 8 (conclusion); Sections 2, 4, 5 skimmed only. Authors are from finQbit and test their own finQbit architecture.
papers.what_it_is: A 2-qubit quantum neural network trained to approximate Black-Scholes-Merton call prices on synthetic data, run on four commercial quantum processors.

assertions.value: The authors report that ibm_fez was the most accurate physical platform, with an R2 exceeding 0.92, and that the compressed ansatz on ibm_fez gave an MSE of 0.000539 and an R2 of 0.9300.
quotes: The IBM Fez processor emerged as the most accurate physical platform, capturing the pricing surface with an R2 exceeding 0.92.
Global Metrics: MSE: 0.000539, R2: 0.9300
assertions.certainty_reason: One study on synthetic Black-Scholes data on a 2-qubit circuit.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 15 puts the ideal simulation at R2 0.9654, so hardware noise costs accuracy even on the best device.

assertions.value: The authors report that the finQbit model kept a predictive R2 above 0.64 on all tested hardware.
quotes: the finQbit model maintained a predictive R2 > 0.64 across all tested hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 15; one study by the architecture's own developers.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 15 lists R2 of 0.6806 (IonQ Forte), 0.6720 (Rigetti Ankaa-3) and 0.6495 (IQM Garnet); the spread between devices is large. The authors are the vendor of the architecture they test.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data are synthetic Black-Scholes-Merton European call prices with a training set of Ntrain = 500 observations and a test set of Ntest = 1001, and that hardware validation used five benchmark points.
quotes: we generated a training set of Ntrain = 500 observations and a test set of Ntest = 1001.
final model performance was validated on physical quantum hardware using five distinct benchmark points
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup, Section 3, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study does not aim to replace classical valuation methods and that the Black-Scholes-Merton model is intentionally simple relative to production models.
quotes: this study does not aim to replace classical valuation methods for standard instruments.
The Black-Scholes-Merton model is intentionally simple relative to the models used in production settings
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit, Section 8, p.18.

papers.title_in_file: Optimizing the Charging of Open Quantum Batteries using Long Short-Term Memory-Driven Reinforcement Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I, V (discussion), VI (conclusions); Sections II to IV (model and RL details) skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A classical deep reinforcement learning controller (DDPG with LSTM) that tunes the charging of a simulated open quantum battery.

assertions.value: The authors report that the RL protocols consistently outperform conventional fixed heuristic strategies by controlling the driving field amplitude and coupling parameters in real time.
quotes: The RL protocols consistently outperform conventional fixed heuristic strategies by real-time controlling the driving field amplitude and coupling parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation study; the comparison is against static controls only.
assertions.reader_inference: The discussion hedges its figure readings (for example 'likely' and 'based on incomplete OCR data'), and the conclusion's figure numbers do not match the figures. The evidence is weaker than the abstract wording.

assertions.value: The authors report DDPG-LSTM training over 10000 updates and, for one parameter set, a maximum extractable work Wmax ranging from 0 to 0.8 and stabilizing near 0.4.
quotes: The training performance of the DDPG-LSTM model is illustrated in Figs. 4 and 5, showing the critic loss and actor loss over 10000 updates.
Figure 6 shows Wmax ranging from 0 to 0.8, stabilizing near 0.4
assertions.certainty_reason: Single simulated run per parameter set.

assertions.value: The authors state that they analyze extractable work in open quantum batteries within the Lindblad master equation framework and build a reinforcement learning framework with a reward function that maximizes extractable work while minimizing backflow.
quotes: we provide a thermodynamic analysis of extractable work in OQBs within the Lindblad master equation framework
featuring a reward function that maximizes extractable work while minimizing backflow
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The system is simulated and the learner is classical; the quantum content is the controlled system, not the model.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Orthogonal Separable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section I, Section V (numerical results text), Section VI (conclusion); Sections II to IV and the appendix proofs skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A separable physics-informed neural network whose layers use quantum orthogonal circuits, with a spectral-normalization-free uncertainty method, tested by classical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using a quantum matrix-multiplication algorithm taken from an earlier reference, the layer's matrix multiplication has log-linear complexity against quadratic classical complexity.
assertions.anchor: Section I, p.1; Section V, p.7
quotes: the log-linear complexity of the QO-SPINN's matrix multiplication to overcome the quadratic complexity of the classical SPINN's matrix multiplication
assertions.certainty_reason: The complexity result comes from the cited quantum algorithm (reference 16 in the paper), not from a new proof here.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup compares asymptotic gate counts; the authors note it needs shot-heavy tomography to read out.

assertions.value: The authors state that on advection-diffusion, Burgers and Sine-Gordon problems the QO-SPINN performs in line with a classical SPINN of similar architecture.
assertions.anchor: Section V, p.7; Section VI, p.9
quotes: In all the tasks QO-SPINN performs in line with SPINN with a similar architecture, as expected.
maintains or surpasses the accuracy standards of classical SPINNs
assertions.certainty_reason: Classical simulation of the quantum circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state that they train the models classically by mapping the quantum circuit to a classical weight matrix, which excludes quantum and statistical noise, and that they compare solution quality rather than speedup.
quotes: We constraint our comparison between QO-SPINN, classical SPINN and PINN to the quality of the retrieved solution rather than on the speedup
This approach excludes any quantum and statistical noise
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states the setup.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum hardware was used and no speedup was measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that the theoretical complexity advantage needs quantum hardware with many high-quality qubits, and that current noise and qubit limits prevent realizing the speedup now.
quotes: current quantum hardware limitations in terms of noise and number of qubits prevent immediate realization of these theoretical speedups in practical applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit, Section VI.

papers.what_it_is: An evolutionary search over parameterized quantum circuit layouts that prunes redundant parameters with the quantum Fisher information matrix, tested on three small classification tasks in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that on Iris EQAS cut the circuit from 5 gates to 1 parameterized gate at 100% accuracy.
quotes: In Iris classification task, the EQAS scheme reduces the number of quantum gates by 80% during searching processing from the initial 5 quantum gates, to finally 1 quantum parameterized gate for 100% accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on a 2-class, 4-feature toy dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that on MNIST the searched circuit reached 94% accuracy with 22 gates of which 9 are parameterized, while Q-NAS reached 96% with 22 parameterized gates.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.5; Appendix C, p.7
quotes: Finally, the searched 4-qubit QCA for the MNIST dataset achieves 94% accuracy with 22 quantum gates which have 9 parameterized gates.
For the same task, the Q-NAS achieves 96% accuracy by 24 quantum parameterized gates included 22 parameterized gates
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on two MNIST classes at 8 by 8 resolution.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract and conclusion claim higher accuracy than Q-NAS, but Table II shows lower final accuracy for EQAS on MNIST (94% against 96%) and Fashion-MNIST (75% against 78%). The gain is in fewer parameterized gates.

assertions.value: The authors state that results come from numerical simulation on 3 classification datasets, with 100 iterations, population size 30 and mutation probability 0.4.
quotes: We demonstrate the numerical simulations of the proposed scheme on 3 classification datasets.
The iterations is 100, the population size is 30 and the mutation probability is 0.4.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup, Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state that Q-NAS achieves higher accuracy at the end of the iterations because it uses more quantum gates.
quotes: But the Q-NAS can achieve a higher accuracy at the end of iterations because the Q-NAS scheme has more quantum gates used in the quantum circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit of the comparison, Section III.

papers.title_in_file: Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit for Hybrid Quantum Systems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Theorem 1 statement, numerical experiments text, Discussion; supplemental proofs skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper proving an algorithm that learns spin-boson Hamiltonian coefficients at the Heisenberg limit, with numerical checks.

assertions.value: The paper states, as its main theorem, an algorithm that estimates all spin-boson Hamiltonian coefficients with total evolution time at the Heisenberg-limit scaling and a polylogarithmic number of measurements, robust to small SPAM error.
quotes: In this paper, we present the first algorithm that learns hybrid Hamiltonians of spin-boson at the Heisenberg limit.
measurements while remaining robust under small SPAM error.
A is robust under small SPAM error.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, p.2, with proofs in the supplement.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is a theoretical scaling; no quantum hardware run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors report that in numerical experiments with small Gaussian noise added to measurements and 6 time points sampled, the estimation error keeps a Heisenberg scaling.
quotes: A small Gaussian noise is added into measurements
and 6 time points are sampled in
We observe that the estimation error maintains a Heisenberg scaling despite the presence of noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation, one noise model.

assertions.value: The authors state that generalizing the protocol to high-dimensional fermionic Hamiltonians and non-linear bosonic modes is left for future exploration.
quotes: For future exploration, one can consider generalizing our learning protocol to high-dimensional fermionic Hamiltonian and non-linear bosonic modes
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated scope limit in the Discussion.
